summary_html: The child is **removed from the home** and placed in foster care under court order or emergency authority. Federal statutes tie funding to safety findings, judicial oversight, and permanency planning.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — removal, reasonable-efforts, and permanency requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal monitoring of placement decisions

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Division of Youth & Family Services v. G.M.
key_cases.holding: The Court held that after a Title 9 abuse-or-neglect finding the parent is entitled to a dispositional hearing on whether the children may safely be returned, and remanded because none was held.
key_cases.relevance: G.M. holds that continued foster placement after a finding requires a dispositional hearing, not automatic continuation.
key_cases.quote: upon a finding of abuse and neglect, the offending parent or guardian is entitled to a dispositional hearing

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. K.L.W.
key_cases.court: New Jersey Superior Court, Appellate Division
key_cases.holding: The court reversed a termination judgment because the Division failed to comply with its statutory duty under N.J.S.A. 30:4C-12.1 to identify and assess relatives, which distorted the best-interests analysis.
key_cases.relevance: K.L.W. holds that non-relative foster placement cannot stand unexamined where identified relatives were never assessed.
key_cases.quote: The Division has a statutory obligation to contact relatives of a child in its custody.

key_cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children and Youth Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for the caseworker, holding that forcing a father from his home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip violated the family's constitutional right to integrity because there were no objectively reasonable grounds to suspect abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Croft governs the constitutional limits on placing a child outside the home without adequate grounds.
key_cases.quote: Even considered together, minor inconsistencies which provide no affirmative evidence of sexual abuse cannot alone establish the objectively reasonable grounds necessary to remove a family member from the family unit.

key_cases.case_name: New Jersey Division of Youth & Family Services v. G.L.
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the termination and ordered reunification, holding DYFS failed to prove the statutory prongs where the mother had never harmed the child and complied with every requirement, and that the fourth prong is a fail-safe against termination rather than an independent basis for it.
key_cases.relevance: G.L. holds that removing a child from a compliant, non-offending parent on the theory that she might someday give the other parent access was improvident and cannot support continued placement.
key_cases.quote: That prong serves as a fail-safe against termination even where the remaining standards have been met.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the dependency adjudication, holding that an unwed father was entitled under the Due Process and Equal Protection Clauses to a hearing on his fitness before the State could take his children from him.
key_cases.relevance: Stanley holds that a child may not be placed in state care on a categorical presumption about the parent, without proof and a hearing.
key_cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

search_keywords: New Jersey Department of Children and Families

state_agency.name: New Jersey Division of Child Protection and Permanency

common_failures: Failure to consider less restrictive alternatives

timeline_requirements.deadline: Hearing on the next court day (the Division must cause a complaint to be filed within two court days after the removal, N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.30(b))
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Child's emergency (“Dodd”) removal from the home without a court order
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: If there has been no hearing on the removal at which the parent or guardian was present or had an adequate opportunity to be present, the parent or guardian may apply for a hearing on returning the child, which must be held within three court days of the application except for good cause shown (N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.32).

notice_requirements.timing: At least 24 hours before the court hearing (reasonable effort by the Division)

statutory_basis.citation_text: N.J.S.A. 9:6-8.30(a) (the Division shall make a reasonable effort, at least 24 hours prior to the court hearing, to notify the parent or guardian of the time to appear in court and to inform the parent or guardian of the right to obtain counsel, and how to obtain counsel through the Office of the Public Defender if indigent)
